question: What does ergodicity economics establish about growth-rate gains from pooling and sharing, and what does it say a pooling instrument should do?

frame.population: multiplicative wealth processes; cooperators; insurance networks
frame.exposure: resource pooling and sharing among agents with multiplicative growth

findings.finding: Expected utility theory and its descendants assume ergodicity indiscriminately; carefully addressing it resolves many economic puzzles in a testable way.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: the prevailing formulations of economic theory — expected utility theory and its descendants — make an indiscriminate assumption of ergodicity.

notFound: The coin-toss gamble numbers and the growth-rate formulae are in the article body, which is behind the journal paywall; the same formulae were read in the preprints below.

item.title: The ergodicity solution of the cooperation puzzle
item.container-title: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society A

findings.finding: Repeated pooling and sharing reduces the effective fluctuation size and raises the time-average growth rate toward the ensemble-average growth rate as cooperators multiply.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Repeated pooling and sharing of resources reduces the effective size of fluctuations and increases the time-average growth rate, which approaches the ensemble-average growth rate in the many-cooperator limit.

findings.finding: The model needs no complementarity or threshold benefit for cooperation to pay.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Classical treatments assume circumstances where combining resources creates an immediate benefit, e.g. through complementarity or thresholds. Here we ask whether cooperation is predictable without such circumstances.

sources.population: resources that self-multiply with fluctuations (viral spread to financial investment)
notFound: Formulae are taken from the preprint row, not from the journal text.

findings.finding: Non-cooperators grow at g = mu - sigma^2/2; N cooperators who pool and share every step grow at g = mu - sigma^2/(2N); the premium is (sigma^2/2)(1 - 1/N), so larger cooperatives are favored.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: ḡ y (N ) = µ − σ²/2N ... The premium increases with the number of cooperators as 1 − 1/N ... implying that larger cooperatives are favored over smaller ones.

findings.finding: With pairwise correlation rho in fluctuations the many-cooperator limit is mu - sigma^2 rho/2: cooperation benefit exists unless fluctuations are perfectly correlated, and relies on diversity of individual outcomes.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: provided fluctuations are not perfectly correlated, a cooperation benefit always exists ... In our setup, cooperation relies on diversity in individual outcomes.

findings.finding: A faster grower should share with a slower grower for N = 2 when mu1 - 3 sigma1^2/4 < mu2 - sigma2^2/4.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: the fast grower should share with the slow grower if µ1 − 3σ1²/4 < µ2 − σ2²/4.

sources.population: N entities with independent multiplicative noisy growth
notFound: Partial cooperation (sharing only a fraction, as in taxation) is deferred in the paper to a separate manuscript.

findings.finding: Judged by time-average growth, a voluntary insurance contract raises both parties growth: shipowner +0.24% per month (1.9% to 2.2%), insurer +0.0071% per month from zero.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: here +0.24% per month ... here +0.0071% per month. Hence, in the time paradigm not only the shipowner but also the insurer should sign the contract.

findings.finding: Expectation-value evaluation makes insurance a zero-sum puzzle; the puzzle goes away under time-average evaluation without utility functions or information asymmetry.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Our reasoning is generalisable: business happens when both parties grow faster.

sources.population: a shipowner of wealth $100,000 and an insurer of wealth $1,000,000 (worked example)

item.title: Cooperation in a non-ergodic world on a network: insurance and beyond

findings.finding: Restricting insurance contracts to lattice neighbours, every agent still profits from cooperating.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: Under these restrictions, we still find that all agents profit from cooperating through insurance.

findings.finding: Clusters of rich and poor agents emerge endogenously and wealth inequality persists for long durations, matching the poverty-trap phenomenon; a rich agent collapses unless other rich agents are nearby to insure it.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: clusters of poor and rich agents emerge endogenously on the two-dimensional map and that wealth inequalities persist for a long duration, consistent with the phenomenon known as the poverty trap.

sources.population: agents on a 64 x 64 periodic square lattice (coordination number four), 200 time units
notFound: Quantitative growth-rate gains per agent are given only in figures.

item.title: Investigating the origins of redistributive behaviour in non-ergodic contexts
item.container-title: Proceedings of the Royal Society A

findings.finding: Participants shared potential gains and losses in multiplicative gambles in ways consistent with time-average growth optimisation rather than expected gain.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: The observed behaviour supports the hypothesis that an element of human decision-making prefers time-average optimization over expected outcomes.

sources.population: human decision-makers, two independent experiments of n = 200 each, 30 multiplicative gambles each
notFound: Country of recruitment and effect sizes not in the abstract.

item.title: The impact of stochastic resetting on resource allocation: the case of reallocating geometric Brownian motion

findings.finding: Optimal resetting balances growth and redistribution and reduces inequality in the resource distribution of reallocating geometric Brownian motion.
findings.exactSourceLanguage: We demonstrate that optimal resetting can effectively balance growth and redistribution, reducing inequality in the resource distribution.
